summary.short: Maryland statute creating consumer personal-data rights and duties for controllers and processors, including notice, consent for sensitive data, opt-outs, processor contracts and data protection assessments, enforced as unfair trade practices. Applies to businesses above volume thresholds; assessment duties apply from 1 October 2025.
summary.long: Maryland's Online Data Privacy Act adds Commercial Law Subtitle 46 (§§ 14-4601 to 14-4614). It covers businesses that conduct business in Maryland or target products or services to residents and that, in the preceding calendar year, processed data of at least 35,000 consumers, or of 10,000 consumers while deriving over 20% of gross revenue from data sales. Controllers must obtain consent for sensitive data, publish privacy notices, honor consumer rights requests within 45 days, and recognize opt-out preference signals. Targeted advertising and sales without consent involving known minors aged 13 to 17 are restricted. Processors must sign binding contracts. Controllers must conduct and document data protection assessments for heightened-risk processing, including each algorithm used. Sale of consumer health data without consent and geofencing near mental or reproductive health facilities are prohibited. Violations are unfair, abusive or deceptive trade practices under Commercial Law Title 13; the Division may issue a notice allowing at least 60 days to cure for violations on or before April 1, 2027. The effective-date clause in Section 4 is marked with both 2024 and 2025. Assessment duties apply to processing from October 1, 2025.

obligations.summary: Where a controller uses a processor, the controller and the processor shall enter into a binding contract setting out processing instructions, nature and purpose, data types, duration and rights and obligations of both parties. The controller shall also provide the processor with instructions on how to process personal data.
obligations.conditional_on: controller uses a processor to process consumers' personal data

evidence.quote: THE CONTROLLER AND THE PROCESSOR SHALL ENTER INTO A CONTRACT THAT GOVERNS THE PROCESSOR’S DATA PROCESSING PROCEDURES

obligations.summary: Under the required contract, the processor shall ensure confidentiality duties for personnel, maintain security practices, stop processing on the controller's request following an authenticated consumer request, delete or return data at the end of service, make compliance information available, engage subcontractors only under a written contract after an opportunity to object, and allow and cooperate with reasonable assessments (with a report on request using an accepted control framework).

evidence.quote: ESTABLISH, IMPLEMENT, AND MAINTAIN REASONABLE ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL DATA SECURITY PRACTICES TO PROTECT THE CONFIDENTIALITY

obligations.summary: A processor shall adhere to the controller's contract and instructions, assist the controller in meeting its obligations (consumer rights requests, security, breach notification) using appropriate technical and organizational measures, and provide necessary information to enable the controller to conduct and document data protection assessments.

evidence.quote: PROVIDE NECESSARY INFORMATION TO ENABLE THE CONTROLLER TO CONDUCT AND DOCUMENT DATA PROTECTION ASSESSMENTS.

obligations.summary: A third party that uses or shares a consumer's information in a manner inconsistent with promises made at collection shall give the affected consumer notice of the new or changed practice before implementing it, in a manner and at a time reasonably calculated to allow the consumer to exercise rights.
obligations.conditional_on: third party uses or shares information inconsistently with promises made at collection

evidence.quote: THE THIRD PARTY SHALL PROVIDE AN AFFECTED CONSUMER WITH NOTICE OF THE NEW OR CHANGED PRACTICE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING THE NEW OR CHANGED PRACTICE.

obligations.summary: A controller that discloses de-identified data shall exercise reasonable oversight to monitor compliance with contractual commitments on that data, and take appropriate steps to address breaches of those commitments, taking into account whether the disclosed data would be sensitive if re-identified.

Demonstration burden is excluded.
